svg.title: PAIA — article-context-en-1440 — design only
svg.desc: Static authored design specification. Fictional examples; not implemented UI or product evidence.

text.tspan: Why keeping your words is only the beginning.
PAIA · Editorial draft for publication review
A useful conversation can still be difficult to return to. You remember that
something became clearer, but not the exact wording, the constraint you
added halfway through, or which of several windows held the decision. The
conversation happened. The continuity did not arrive automatically.
That gap is where we place PAIA. Not in front of every conversation, asking
you to prepare a perfect brief. Not above your words, deciding who you are.
Beside them: a working place to find an earlier expression, see where it
came from and decide whether it still belongs in the next step.
Keeping everything is not the same as using something well. A long archive
may contain questions you no longer have, quotations you never agreed
with, and plans that were deliberately abandoned. Bringing all of it into a new
task can obscure the very context you were trying to recover.
Selection matters. So does the ability to revise. You may want the original
record to remain intact while making today’s working explanation shorter and
clearer. These are compatible needs when the source and the working
version do not pretend to be the same thing.
In this model, context is not a secret profile that a system accumulates about
you. It is material you can inspect and deliberately bring to a particular
question. The useful amount may be three sentences rather than three
years. The relevant version may be the one you edited this morning.
PAIA starts with expressions you already produce in AI conversations. Its
ambition is continuity without a maintenance habit: less reconstruction, more
room to continue. Capture, revisit, understand, reuse. Not a compulsory
sequence, but a set of ways to make past thinking available when it
A product perspective, not a claim of released capability.
Your thinking has a longer tomorrow.
Photography credits · Illustrative material, not a live archive
